1.pericope_label: And David spake unto the Lord the words of this song in the day that the Lord had delivered him out of the hand of all his enemies, and out of the hand of Saul: And he said, The Lord is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; The God of my rock; in him will I trust: he is my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my high tower, and my refuge, my saviour; thou savest me from violence. I will call on the Lord, who is worthy to be praised: so shall I be saved from mine enemies. When the waves of death compassed me, the floods of ungodly men made me afraid; The sorrows of hell compassed me about; the snares of death prevented me; In my distress I called upon the Lord, and cried to my God: and he did hear my voice out of his temple, and my cry did enter into his ears.

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the comparison with the eighteenth psalm his whole method and begins where the difference begins, noting that the psalm's opening line about loving the Lord his strength is wanting here though it forms a fitting introduction, that the omission is partly compensated by the words on refuge and saviour and deliverance from violence which stand here and not there, that the two expressions the psalm keeps separate are here united in one, and that the recurrence of the united phrase near the end of this chapter but not of the psalm shows the change was intentional; on the cry he observes that where the psalm has the bands of death this chapter has the waves, an entirely different word whose variation can hardly have been accidental. Delitzsch sets out the architecture rather than the variants, taking the opening verses for an introduction containing the sum and substance of the whole, and renders the strophe of distress as breakers of death compassing him about with cords of hell girding him and snares of death overtaking him.

Clarke states the consequence of the duplication bluntly, that since the substance and almost the words are the same the exposition must be reserved for the psalm, and confines himself to a very few observations; but he raises the chapter's deepest question by reproducing at length an argument that the poetry cannot be perfectly understood until it is known who the speaker is, since if the person is David only the Messiah is excluded and the apostle who quotes part of it as predicting the conversion of the Gentiles is contradicted, while the difficulties on either side have led to the general idea that it relates to both. Clarke's own position is firmer: though in a primary sense many of these things belong to David, generally and fully they belong to the Messiah alone.

Henry reads the titles as a series of answers to particular distresses, holding that all others adored as deities are counterfeits and pretenders since they are dead while the Lord lives and disappoint their worshippers when most needed, and that men begin in kindness but do not end while God will finish his work; from the single confession that he is my God he derives the rest, the rock that is as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land, the fortress in which I am safe and think myself so, the high tower out of reach of real evils, and then deliverer, shield, refuge, saviour and horn of salvation answering in turn to distress, assault, pursuit and oppression.

debates: Who the speaker of the psalm is, which Clarke raises as the question on which everything turns, since if it is David only the Messiah is excluded while the description is hard to fit to David, and which he answers by giving the primary sense to David and the full sense to the Messiah alone.

How the two recensions stand to each other, where Ellicott treats every divergence as evidence of distinct recensions while Clarke treats the duplication as a reason to defer exposition to the psalm altogether.
What the opening verses are doing, which Delitzsch takes for an introduction containing the sum and substance of the whole psalm, while Ellicott reads them as the first site of textual divergence.
outliers: Ellicott notes that the words here about refuge and saviour and deliverance from violence have no counterpart in the psalm, and are partly compensated there by the opening line this chapter lacks.
Henry derives the whole series of divine titles from the single confession that he is my God, treating each as the answer to a particular distress.

8.pericope_label: Then the earth shook and trembled; the foundations of heaven moved and shook, because he was wroth. There went up a smoke out of his nostrils, and fire out of his mouth devoured: coals were kindled by it. He bowed the heavens also, and came down; and darkness was under his feet. And he rode upon a cherub, and did fly: and he was seen upon the wings of the wind. And he made darkness pavilions round about him, dark waters, and thick clouds of the skies. Through the brightness before him were coals of fire kindled. The Lord thundered from heaven, and the most High uttered his voice. And he sent out arrows, and scattered them; lightning, and discomfited them. And the channels of the sea appeared, the foundations of the world were discovered, at the rebuking of the Lord, at the blast of the breath of his nostrils. He sent from above, he took me; he drew me out of many waters; He delivered me from my strong enemy, and from them that hated me: for they were too strong for me. They prevented me in the day of my calamity: but the Lord was my stay. He brought me forth also into a large place: he delivered me, because he delighted in me.

schools.summary: Ellicott catalogues the divergences of the theophany as evidence rather than curiosities: where this chapter has the foundations of heaven shaken the psalm has the foundations of the hills, the strong figure calling the mountains the pillars of heaven being softened there; where this chapter has the Lord seen upon the wings of the wind the psalm has him flying, two words exceedingly alike in the Hebrew of which the psalm's is far the more poetical; a word appears to have dropped out of the verse about darkness, where he also prefers the margin's gathering of waters. From the several slight differences he concludes that they mark the two as distinctly different recensions, and he singles out the shift of the final pronoun from his to thy in the psalm as appropriate to its use in public worship. Delitzsch works the same ground harder, finding that the received vowel reading obliterates a significant alternation of verbal forms, that this text has the heavens where the psalm has the mountains by an extension of the figure meant of the points of support of the heavens themselves, and that the verse about the brightness is terribly mutilated, only four letters surviving of the clause the other text preserves.

Clarke stops for one verse only and for a reason neither of the others gives, finding in the line about riding upon a cherub that sense and sound are astonishingly well connected, setting out the Hebrew word by word so that an unlearned reader may hear it, and observing that the clap of the wing and the rush through the air are expressed in a very extraordinary manner.

Henry declines the textual question and asks instead why the language of Sinai is used at all, since in none of David's battles did God fight for him with thunder as in Samuel's time or with hail as in Joshua's or with the stars in their courses as in Deborah's; he answers with four purposes, that the metaphors set forth the glory of God, which appearing for David was as clear a discovery to an eye of faith as miracles would have been to an eye of sense, his displeasure, since he so espoused David's cause as to show himself an enemy to all his enemies, the confusion of the enemies, as if the earth had trembled and the foundations of the world been discovered, and his readiness to help, hastening to David's succour though he had seemed at a distance. On the close he fastens on the reason given, that the deliverance came not from common providence but from covenant love.

debates: Which recension preserves the better poetry in the theophany, where Ellicott repeatedly prefers the psalm, finding its figure of flight more poetical and its account of the darkness fuller, while holding this chapter's pillars of heaven the stronger figure that the psalm softens.

What has happened to the verse about the brightness, which Delitzsch calls terribly mutilated with only four letters of the other text surviving, while Ellicott reads what stands and simply prefers out of the brightness to through it.

Why the language of Sinai is used of battles in which no such wonders occurred, which Henry raises directly and answers with four purposes the metaphors serve, none of them requiring a literal convulsion.
outliers: Clarke finds in the line about the cherub that sense and sound are astonishingly well connected, the clap of the wing and the rush through the air being audible in the Hebrew itself.
Delitzsch denies that the pillars of heaven are meant of mountains holding the sky up, taking them for the points of support of the heavens themselves, so that the whole universe trembles.

21.pericope_label: The Lord rewarded me according to my righteousness: according to the cleanness of my hands hath he recompensed me. For I have kept the ways of the Lord, and have not wickedly departed from my God. For all his judgments were before me: and as for his statutes, I did not depart from them. I was also upright before him, and have kept myself from mine iniquity. Therefore the Lord hath recompensed me according to my righteousness; according to my cleanness in his eye sight. With the merciful thou wilt shew thyself merciful, and with the upright man thou wilt shew thyself upright. With the pure thou wilt shew thyself pure; and with the froward thou wilt shew thyself unsavoury. And the afflicted people thou wilt save: but thine eyes are upon the haughty, that thou mayest bring them down. For thou art my lamp, O Lord: and the Lord will lighten my darkness. For by thee I have run through a troop: by my God have I leaped over a wall. As for God, his way is perfect; the word of the Lord is tried: he is a buckler to all them that trust in him. For who is God, save the Lord? and who is a rock, save our God? God is my strength and power: and he maketh my way perfect. He maketh my feet like hinds’ feet: and setteth me upon my high places. He teacheth my hands to war; so that a bow of steel is broken by mine arms. Thou hast also given me the shield of thy salvation: and thy gentleness hath made me great. Thou hast enlarged my steps under me; so that my feet did not slip.

schools.summary: Delitzsch is at his most severe on the text here, noting that the form used for my righteousness is contrary to the usage of the Psalms, that a poetical construction found in Job has been replaced by a common prose phrase, that one reading has no example elsewhere since the usual expression for innocence speaks of the hands, and that a verb form has only the sound of the reflexive it appears to be; at the verse about the lamp he finds a word lost outright, the spelling of the surviving word wavering incorrectly between two forms and the repetition of the divine name that covers the loss inelegant, and at the verse about gentleness he finds the five-line stanza stunted by the falling away of its middle line. Ellicott traces the same divergences without the asperity and twice prefers the psalm on poetic grounds, reading froward for unsavoury and my strong fortress for God is my strength and power, and agreeing with Delitzsch that the word for gentleness is otherwise unknown and would by its etymology mean thy answering to the prayers offered.

Henry reads the section as a question of what the deliverances were for and finds the answer in the enlargement that followed, holding that God sometimes brings his people into very great difficulties that he may have the honour of saving them and they the comfort of being saved by him, and that the deliverance is magnified by the greatness of the danger, since the singer could no more help himself than a man in the grave can. The successes he treats as a second mercy on the first, since David was brought into a large place where he had room to thrive and his steps were enlarged under him so that he had room to stir; and from the plea of integrity he takes an improvement of the relation rather than a defence of the claim, that if God be mine then in him will I trust and on him will I call.

debates: Whether the text of this section can be trusted as it stands, where Delitzsch finds a lost word, an unexampled reading, an anomalous verb form and a stunted stanza, while Ellicott treats the same places as slight variations and decides them on grounds of parallelism and poetic effect.

What the word rendered gentleness means, which Delitzsch and Ellicott agree is otherwise unknown and would by etymology mean thy answering, that is, the actual help with which the prayer was answered.

What the plea of integrity is doing in a psalm of thanksgiving, which Henry turns from a claim about David into an improvement of the relation, trust and prayer following from the confession that God is mine.
outliers: Delitzsch holds that a word has been lost from the verse about the lamp, since the divine name is called light in the Psalms but never lamp, and that the repetition which covers the loss is inelegant.
Henry reads the lamp as question and answer in one: am I in the dark, benighted, at a loss, then thou art my lamp to show me my way.

38.pericope_label: I have pursued mine enemies, and destroyed them; and turned not again until I had consumed them. And I have consumed them, and wounded them, that they could not arise: yea, they are fallen under my feet. For thou hast girded me with strength to battle: them that rose up against me hast thou subdued under me. Thou hast also given me the necks of mine enemies, that I might destroy them that hate me. They looked, but there was none to save; even unto the Lord, but he answered them not. Then did I beat them as small as the dust of the earth, I did stamp them as the mire of the street, and did spread them abroad. Thou also hast delivered me from the strivings of my people, thou hast kept me to be head of the heathen: a people which I knew not shall serve me. Strangers shall submit themselves unto me: as soon as they hear, they shall be obedient unto me. Strangers shall fade away, and they shall be afraid out of their close places. The Lord liveth; and blessed be my rock; and exalted be the God of the rock of my salvation. It is God that avengeth me, and that bringeth down the people under me, And that bringeth me forth from mine enemies: thou also hast lifted me up on high above them that rose up against me: thou hast delivered me from the violent man. Therefore I will give thanks unto thee, O Lord, among the heathen, and I will sing praises unto thy name. He is the tower of salvation for his king: and sheweth mercy to his anointed, unto David, and to his seed for evermore.

schools.summary: Delitzsch finds the same kind of loss through the victories, and they are losses of art rather than sense: where the psalter has the singer overtaking his enemies this text has him destroying them, by which the echo of the song at the sea is obliterated, the following clause is tautological, and the two figures about the dust and the mire appear here in a distorted form; at the doxology the change of position of the divine name is against the rhythm and the shortened verb both against the rhythm and contrary to custom. Ellicott reads the same divergences as mostly scribal and once as designed, calling they looked against they cried a clerical error, but judging the psalm's compact figure of dust before the wind a designed change that heightens the poetic effect, and ending on the variant in which a transposed letter leaves the conquered coming trembling from their fastnesses in the psalm and coming limping here, as though the remnant had already been wounded. He closes with a lesson in providence, that the review of the two recensions shows the manuscripts of the Old Testament secured through long ages from all substantial error while mere slips of the pen crept in, so that care and diligence are required to establish what was first written.

Henry ends on the publicity of the praise rather than on the text, since among the heathen David would neither be afraid nor ashamed to own his obligations to the God of Israel; and he closes the psalm with the titles he opened it with, that the Lord is the horn and the rock of salvation, David's saving strength being in him and from him, and that the tower of salvation can never be scaled nor battered nor undermined, since salvation itself saves him.

debates: Whether the divergences in this section are accidents or improvements, where Ellicott calls most of them clerical errors but judges the psalm's figure of dust before the wind a designed change that heightens the effect, while Delitzsch reads the whole series as losses of art.

What the comparison of the two recensions finally shows, which Ellicott turns into a statement about providence and the manuscripts, that they were secured from substantial error without ordinary human slips being prevented.
Where the psalm ends, which for Henry is in public thanksgiving among the heathen and in the titles the psalm began with, and for Delitzsch in a doxology whose rhythm this recension has damaged.
outliers: Ellicott ends on the finest of the variants, a transposed letter which leaves the conquered coming trembling from their fastnesses in the psalm and coming limping here, suggesting the remnant had already been injured.
Delitzsch calls the word for rock thrust into the verse about the living Lord simply troublesome.
